newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian political crisis clouds talks with Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Indian political crisis clouds talks with Pakistan.

text.p: Indian and Pakistani diplomats held a third day of talks on Sunday, but a political crisis in New Delhi cast doubt on the future of the dialogue.

Sitaram Kesri, the leader of India's Congress party, said it had withdrawn support for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's nine-month-old minority coalition government -- though there was no sign that the move was connected with the Pakistan talks.
It was not immediately clear if the Congress decision would lead to new elections or an immediate change of government.
Either way, the political upheaval added a new complication to the renewal of a fragile dialogue between India and Pakistan, long at bitter odds over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.
Officials said Pakistan's foreign secretary Shamshad Ahmad and his Indian counterpart Salman Haidar met in New Delhi for the first of Sunday's two scheduled sessions.
The meeting went ahead despite renewed violence in the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir.
A car bomb blast in the state's winter capital Jammu killed 16 people and wounded about 70 on Saturday. Farooq Abdullah, the chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir, blamed Pakistan.
"This dastardly act was sponsored by Pakistan's ISI (Inter-Services Intelligence) and its agents with the intention of dividing the people on communal lines," he said.
"The ISI doesn't want normalisation of relations between India and Pakistan and is...trying to create trouble in a bid to divide communities to further its ends," his statement added.
Jammu, winter capital of India's Moslem-majority state of Jammu and Kashmir, is populated mainly by Hindus.
No one has claimed responsibility for the attack and there has been no comment from Pakistan on Abdullah's allegation.

Nine policemen were wounded on Sunday when a device tied to the body of a slain guerrilla exploded at a police station in Kupwara, near the India-Pakistan border 87 km (55 miles) north of Srinagar, the state's summer capital, police said.
The India-Pakistan talks, reviving a dialogue that collapsed in January 1994 over Kashmir, have been shrouded in secrecy, with participants saying very little about their progress.

Pakistani spokesman Khalid Saleem said the two sides had discussed "all substantive issues" on Saturday, including the thorny issue of Kashmir, over which India and Pakistan have fought two of their three wars since independence in 1947.
Pakistan, which advocates a plebiscite in Kashmir to let its people choose whether to join India or Pakistan, wants "some progress" on the dispute before other issues can be tackled.

India says its sovereignty over Kashmir is not negotiable and has proposed putting the decades-old quarrel on the back burner. It would like agreements on promoting trade and economic cooperation and other confidence-building measures.
The main Kashmiri separatist leader said after meeting Ahmad on Saturday evening that the talks seemed unlikely to succeed.

Mirwaiz Omar Farooq, chairman of the All Parties Hurriyat (freedom) Conference, told Reuters he had protested to the Pakistanis about what he said was Islamabad's failure to consult Kashmiris before renewing the dialogue with India.
"We said this is not the right time," Farooq said. India should first have showed its sincerity by reducing violence in the mainly Moslem Kashmir Valley. "This did not happen."
Farooq said Indian assertions that Kashmir was a closed chapter indicated that Delhi was "posturing".
He said the Pakistani delegation did not expect the talks to produce any breakthrough on the disputed territory.
"It is obvious that India is not ready to budge an inch from their stand on Kashmir," he declared.
